metric_rationale: The design contains four trial types (T7-T10) on which the two options split feature-wise wins exactly evenly (1-1 or 2-2), so the Tallying softmax is mathematically uniform for ANY beta and epsilon: Tallying must choose the highest-validity-cue winner exactly 50% of the time, with only binomial noise (32 such trials per subject => between-subject SD ~0.09). Take The Best, in contrast, resolves these pairs on the first discriminating cue and therefore chooses the top-cue winner with probability (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2, which for essentially the whole plausible parameter range sits well above chance (~0.80-0.95). The metric is the proportion of tally-tie trials on which the option favored by the highest-validity discriminating cue was chosen. It is parameter-free for Tallying (fixed at 0.5, tight across subjects) and clearly above 0.5 for TTB, giving a large mean gap with modest per-subject variability. It also works identically on a single subject's slice and on the pooled data, and side/direction counterbalancing in the design ensures response bias cannot inflate it.

The design contains conflict trials in which the tally winner and the one-reason (TTB) winner are opposite options, and where the tally margin is large (|M| >= 2): trials 1/2 (A wins the .93 expert but loses the tally 1-4) and trials 11/12 (the two best experts tie so TTB descends to f2 and picks one option, while the tally favors the other by 2). This metric is the proportion of choices on exactly those trials that agree with the tally winner.

Prediction under Tallying: with margin magnitude 2-3, softmax choice is near-deterministic for the tally winner for almost the whole beta range, so the score is (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*|M|)+eps/2, i.e. near 0.85-1.0. Prediction under TTB: exactly the complement, eps/2 + (1-eps)*(1-sigmoid(beta)), i.e. near 0-0.15. The expected mean gap is ~0.7-0.75 while per-subject variance is small (only lapse-rate spread plus binomial noise over 32 trials at extreme p), which is what Welch's test at N=25 needs. Restricting to |M| >= 2 avoids the weak M=1 cells where Tallying's own prediction is soft; excluding agreement and tie cells removes trials where the two theories predict the same thing and which would only dilute the contrast.

This is the overall adherence rate to the full-tally winner (the option that wins on strictly more features), pooled over the 96 trials of the design (every trial in this design has a non-zero tally margin, so no trial is dropped).

Why it separates the theories: LSNC's core commitment is that only a small, randomly drawn subset of cues (mean k between 1.5 and 3.5 of the 6 features) is ever inspected, that tied cues occupy sampling slots (tie dilution), and that each inspected comparison is mis-registered with probability nu = .12-.32. A small noisy sample frequently reverses or fails to recover the sign of the global margin, so LSNC's adherence is structurally CAPPED: exact enumeration for this design gives ~0.57-0.75 across the six cells, i.e. an aggregate near 0.65-0.68, and it cannot approach 1 for any admissible parameter setting. Tallying, in contrast, reads every feature and passes the exact margin (M = 1, 2 or 3 here, never 0) through a softmax; over the bulk of its inverse-temperature range the softmax is essentially deterministic, so its adherence sits near 1 - epsilon/2, i.e. roughly 0.85-0.90 on average and never structurally attenuated by the composition of the profile.

This is not trivially true of my theory: Tallying is perfectly free to produce low adherence (small beta, large epsilon), and LSNC is free to produce moderately high adherence (large k, small nu) - the metric measures a behavioural ceiling, not a theory label. The prediction that humans in a 6-cue, feedback-free, high-conflict task fall far short of margin-consistent responding (adherence well below 0.8 even at margin 3) is the substantive LSNC claim; Tallying, which by construction integrates all cues, has to attribute any such shortfall to a degenerate temperature that would then also flatten the margin gradient. The metric is a simple proportion over ~96 trials per subject, so its per-subject sampling noise is small (sd ~0.04-0.05), keeping the between-subject variance tight relative to the ~0.2 mean gap.

The single sharpest quantitative divergence between the two accounts is the ATTAINABLE LEVEL of adherence to the complete-profile tally winner on clearly discriminating pairs. Every trial in this design has a strict global tally winner with margin M = 2 or M = 4, and (by construction) the option favoured by the tally also wins the most valid cue, so the metric is not confounded by cue-order strategies.

Under softmax Tallying the decision variable is the FULL margin: P(winner) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*M) + eps/2. Since M >= 2 on every trial, sigmoid(beta*M) is already essentially at ceiling for most of the beta range, so adherence is pinned near 1 - eps/2, i.e. roughly 0.85-0.90 on average and, crucially, only weakly dispersed (its across-subject spread comes from the lapse parameter alone, since 48 + 48 trials wash out binomial noise).

Under LSNC the inspected subset averages ~2.5 of 8 cues and each comparison is mis-registered with prob nu ~ 0.2, so a large global margin is routinely reversed or diluted by tied cues occupying sampling slots. Exact enumeration for this design gives adherence ~0.60-0.66 at M=2 and ~0.69-0.75 at M=4, i.e. a pooled value around 0.66-0.70 that is CAPPED well below what full integration produces, and again tightly distributed across subjects because the parameter ranges (k in [1.5,3.5], nu in [0.12,0.32]) move it only a few points.

So the expected contrast is roughly 0.87 vs 0.68 with per-subject variances of order 0.005-0.008 in both cases, which at N=25 is a very large Welch t. This is not trivially true of Tallying: had subjects been strongly noise-limited, Tallying's own epsilon/beta would drag adherence down toward the LSNC band; the prediction that adherence sits high above the sample-limited ceiling is a substantive commitment of full-cue integration.

The design holds the win-count composition (nA,nB,nT) exactly fixed while flipping whether the highest-validity expert (0.94) sides with or against the count winner. LSNC (advocated) samples cues uniformly at random, so its predicted adherence depends only on (nA,nB,nT) and is mathematically invariant to which cues the winner owns: the coherent-minus-conflict adherence difference is exactly 0 for every parameter setting (k, nu, epsilon). CDCC gates confidence through the convex validity-weighted coherence term C, with kappa >= 0.4 by hypothesis, so it must show a large positive gap (~0.15, i.e. ~0.71 coherent vs ~0.56 conflict). Each subject supplies 48 coherent and 48 conflict trials, so the within-subject difference has SE ~0.10, giving a very tight per-subject estimate and a between-theory separation of many standard errors at N=25. Side mirrors within each cell cancel any side bias, and the coherence label is derived generically (winner owns the most valid discriminating cue), so no trial-index bookkeeping is required.

Two structurally signed contrasts are summed, each of which has an opposite (or null) sign under the two theories, so the composite separates them with a large mean gap while each component is estimated from 32/32 and 16/16 trials per subject (tight per-subject noise).

D1 = adherence(count-winner) on validity-COHERENT conflicting profiles minus adherence on validity-INCOHERENT profiles, with the (nA,nB,nT) composition held EXACTLY matched across the two sets by design (T1/T2 vs T3/T4 both (2,1,4); T5/T6 vs T7/T8 both (4,2,1)). LSNC samples cues uniformly and ignores validity entirely, so its predicted adherence depends only on (nA,nB,nT): D1 = 0 exactly, for every k, nu, epsilon. CDCC gates confidence by the convex validity-weighted coherence C, so D1 is strictly positive (~+0.11 to +0.17, larger for larger kappa) and cannot be turned off.

D2 = adherence on the UNANIMOUS-SPARSE profile (2 winning cues, 0 opposing, 5 tied) minus adherence on the UNANIMOUS-DENSE profile (4 winning cues, 0 opposing, 3 tied). For CDCC the dilution term S = M/D^gamma gives 2^(1-gamma) vs 4^(1-gamma) = (2^(1-gamma))^2, and since gamma > 1 the sparse profile ALWAYS yields the larger confidence: D2 >= 0 for every admissible parameter vector. For LSNC tied cues waste sampling slots, so the dense profile (4/7 informative slots) always beats the sparse one (2/7): D2 < 0 (~ -0.06 to -0.12) for every admissible parameter vector.

Hence the composite D1 + D2 is bounded below by 0 under CDCC (expected ~ +0.18) and is expected to be clearly negative under LSNC (~ -0.09), a gap of roughly 0.27 with per-subject variance dominated by binomial sampling over 96 trials (sd ~ 0.17), which gives a Welch t well above 4 at N=25. It is not trivially true for CDCC: a flat coherence effect or an ordering with dense > sparse on unanimous profiles would push the metric to zero/negative and falsify it.

The design contains exactly four cells in which the high-validity 'star' tier (f0=.95, f2=.88, f5=.83) and the low-validity 'marginal' tier (f1=.57, f3=.60, f4=.66) point in OPPOSITE directions: C3 (1 star vs 1 marginal, tally-tied), C4 (2 stars vs 2 marginals, tally-tied), C5 (3 stars vs 2 marginals, count favours the star side) and C6 (3 marginals vs 2 stars, count favours the marginal side). The metric is the overall rate of choosing the option backed by the LOW-validity marginal tier on exactly those trials (64 of the 96 trials per subject, mirrored so side bias cancels exactly).

RDTI-MCR treats the star tier as redundant restatement (residual weight eps_w) and additionally applies a contrarian discount proportional to the count margin. In all four cells the discriminating panel is dense (D>=2), so the graded redundancy release is essentially zero and the star tier stays discounted. Across the entire declared parameter box this yields marginal-tier adherence of roughly .73-.93 (C3), .82-.97 (C4), .82-.97 (C5, i.e. sub-chance adherence to the count winner) and ~.88-.95 (C6) — an overall metric near .85-.95.

CDCC is pinned near .5: on C3 and C4 the tallies are equal, so it must be EXACTLY .5 for every parameter setting; on C5 the count winner is the star-backed option and its coherence gate is near 1, giving marginal-tier adherence of only ~.29-.40; on C6 the coherence gate collapses (best cues oppose the count) so it barely exceeds chance, ~.50-.55. Averaging gives ~.44-.51.

So the predicted gap is ~0.40-0.45 with each subject contributing 64 trials (binomial SD ~0.06) and both theories being parametrically tight in this contrast, giving a very large Welch t. Crucially the metric is not trivially true of RDTI: any tallying, WADD, take-the-best, or validity-weighted account predicts values at or below .5 here (it requires systematically siding with the least valid experts), so the contrast is a genuine, falsifiable behavioural signature rather than a restatement of the model.

This is the sign-reversal diagnostic (design cells C3 and C6): dense/mid displays (D>=4) with a feature-count majority whose supporting cues are exactly the high-validity 'star' experts while the count loser is supported only by low-validity marginal experts. The metric is the proportion of such trials on which the subject chooses the count winner (32 of 96 trials per subject, so binomial noise per subject is ~0.008 in variance).

CDCC makes direction purely count-based and floors the confidence argument at zero, so adherence must be strictly above 0.5 here, and because coherence is maximal (all star weight on the winner's side) the gate is near 1: across its whole parameter box the predicted adherence is roughly 0.57-0.92, centred near 0.70-0.75.

RDTI-MCR discounts precisely the star tier (residual weight eps_w<=0.34, and its graded redundancy release is inert at D>=2) and additionally applies a contrarian discount proportional to the count margin, so the tier-weighted evidence 4*eps_w-2 (C3) and 3*eps_w-1 (C6) is negative and the majority discount pushes further down: predicted adherence is roughly 0.02-0.35, centred near 0.13.

So the two theories are separated not just in magnitude but in sign relative to chance (~0.73 vs ~0.15), with tight per-subject estimates (32 trials each and a narrow parameter-induced spread), which should yield a very large Welch t at N=25. It is not trivially true of CDCC: any model that lets high-validity cues drive direction (WADD/TTB) would also score high here, and any model that discounts them scores low; the metric measures a directional signature, not a parameter of my model.

The metric is the proportion of dense-display trials (D>=2 discriminating cues) on which the subject chooses the option favoured by the net vote of the LOW-validity (bottom-half) experts f1(.78), f4(.76), f3(.55). This single number is defined stimulus-wise (no trial indices needed), applies to 64 of the 96 trials per subject, and is well defined for a single subject's slice, so it is tight per subject (mostly binomial noise over 64 trials plus modest parameter spread).

Why it discriminates: RDTI-MCR gives the whole bottom tier weight 1 and the star tier weight eps_w<=0.34, and additionally subtracts a contrarian majority discount, so on all four dense cells it follows the marginal-tier-backed option: K1 ~0.86, K2 ~0.93, K3 ~0.81, K4 ~0.84 (adherence 0.75-0.95 over its whole parameter box) => pooled value ~0.86.

GVIT-CAP-S4 behaves very differently on exactly these trials. On the two tally-tied cells (K1, K2, 32 trials) its count gate returns EXACTLY 0.5 for every parameter setting, so adherence is chance. On K3 its strongly saturating inversion makes f1/f4 nearly as discounted as the stars while the lone floor expert f3 keeps full weight, reversing the choice (adherence ~0.12). On K4 the floor expert again pulls toward the star-backed side (adherence ~0.38). Pooled value ~0.37-0.40.

Expected gap ~0.48 with per-subject variance on the order of 0.005 for both theories, giving a Welch t of roughly 20 at N=25. Crucially the metric is not trivially true for RDTI: any model that weights cues monotonically in stated validity (the normative/classic weighted-additive account) would score far BELOW 0.5, and GVIT's own inverse-validity account scores below 0.5 too; only RDTI's coarse two-tier split at the .80/.78 boundary plus majority discounting produces a high value.

This is a within-subject double contrast built from the two cells where the models make opposite-signed, near-parameter-free commitments, so the individual gaps ADD rather than cancel.

Cell C3 (trials 5/6): exactly two cues favour each option (bottom pair f2=.55,f5=.52 vs stars f1=.95,f6=.90). GVIT-CAP-S4's count gate fires on nA=nB and returns EXACTLY 0.5 with no validity tie-break, for every parameter setting: P(choose bottom-backed) = 0.50. RDTI-MCR weights the marginal tier fully and the star tier at eps_w, with margin=0 so the contrarian discount is inert, giving a strong pull toward the bottom-backed option (~0.85-0.96 across its whole parameter box).

Cell C4 (trials 7/8): the mid pair (f0=.74,f4=.70) opposes the lone floor expert (f5=.52). GVIT's strongly saturating inversion makes the mid pair nearly worthless (or counter-indicative) while the floor voice keeps full weight, so subjects should follow the single .52 expert: P(follow floor) ~ 0.65-0.90. RDTI puts all three cues in the marginal tier, so E = +1 exactly and, despite the count discount, it follows the mid-pair majority: P(follow floor) ~ 0.08-0.28.

Taking (follow-floor in C4) minus (bottom-backed in C3) makes the two signs oppose: GVIT ~ +0.35, RDTI ~ -0.75, a gap of ~1.1 on a bounded [-1,1] scale. Each subject contributes 16 trials to each cell, so the per-subject sampling variance of the difference is at most ~0.03 (SD ~0.18), which is tiny relative to the gap. The metric is computed identically on a single subject's slice and on the pooled frame, and mirrored A/B versions of each configuration are pooled by identifying the target option structurally (which side wins the bottom pair / the floor cue), so any side bias cancels exactly.

Composite of three cell-level adherence contrasts, each of which has an analytically guaranteed sign difference between the two models at n_features=6 (both models' panel-size terms are inert here), averaged to shrink binomial noise.

(1) LONE-VOICE contrast (D3 - C2): the majority (the .84 and .78 experts) is held exactly fixed and only the identity of the single dissenter changes (.95 vs .68). Under SR-DT a lone voice is boosted above face value with a seniority-graded bonus, so the star dissenter is at least as damaging as the floor dissenter: the contrast is necessarily <= 0 (simulated ~-0.02 to -0.05, both cells near the floor). Under GVIT the lone voice's weight is 1 - lam_eff*s^omega with v_min anchoring, so the .68 dissenter carries weight exactly +1 while the .95 dissenter carries 1 - lam_eff < 0: the contrast is necessarily large and POSITIVE (~+0.32 to +0.54 across its whole parameter box).

(2) E4 adherence (majority = .95,.90,.68 vs .78,.72): SR-DT's chance-baselined superlinear discount makes the star-backed majority counter-indicative (~0.15-0.30), whereas GVIT's floor-anchored weights give the .68 voice full weight that offsets the two discounted stars, landing at ~0.45-0.60.

(3) Reversed A1 adherence (1 - follow of the mid-trio majority): SR-DT leaves the middling experts substantial positive news value (~0.72 adherence -> term ~0.28); GVIT's strongly concave s^omega nearly nullifies them while the .68 voice on the other side keeps full weight (~0.32 adherence -> term ~0.68).

All three terms point the same way (GVIT high, SR-DT low), each is computed from 16 trials per subject, and each is tight within its own parameter box, so the pooled score should be ~0.15 for SR-DT vs ~0.55 for GVIT with small between-subject variance. Nothing here is trivially true of SR-DT: it is a measured cross-cell pattern that either model could in principle produce.

This isolates the single most diagnostic cell of the design (K4, trials 7/8 and their exact mirrors): a three-cue majority carried by the low-mid experts (.72, .58, .68) opposed by exactly ONE dissenting cue, and that dissenter is the panel's floor voice (.52). The metric is the proportion of those 16 trials on which the subject follows the 3-cue count majority; because both A-favouring and B-favouring mirrors are pooled, side bias cancels exactly.

GVIT-CAP-S4 and SR-DT-6b make opposite-sided predictions here, for structural reasons rather than parameter fine-tuning. Under GVIT, the redundancy discount is strongly concave (omega<1) and its chorus criterion uses the TOTAL number of discriminating cues, so all three mid-level supporters are discounted almost to zero news value while the lone .52 dissenter (panel-relative s = 0 exactly, weight 1.0, parameter-free) retains full weight: E is negative across essentially the whole parameter box, giving sub-chance adherence (~0.2). Under SR-DT, seniority is anchored at chance, the discount is superlinear (so sub-.80 experts keep most of their voice), redundancy is same-side only, and the lone floor dissenter gets only ~phi0 weight; unopposed-ish majorities are further sharpened by the dissent divisor, yielding near-ceiling adherence (~0.9). A 3-vs-1 count majority being REJECTED is impossible anywhere in SR-DT's box.

Each subject contributes 16 trials to the estimate, so within-subject binomial noise is small (<=0.016 variance) and the predicted between-theory gap (~0.7) is many standard errors wide at N=25. I advocate GVIT and predict a value near 0.2; the competitor must predict near 0.9.

The two models differ structurally only in whether a 'redundant' (high-validity) expert is MUTE (CG-VI-2: news value floored at zero) or COUNTER-INDICATIVE (GVIT: weights go negative). That difference can only show up on displays in which the discriminating voices are ALL appreciably above the panel floor, i.e. where no low-validity maverick (0.55 or 0.63) speaks. This metric selects exactly those trials (all discriminating features have validity >= 0.72, and a strict count winner exists) and scores adherence to the plain count winner. In this design those are the A1 (T1/T2, unopposed star pair, 2-0), A3 (T5/T6, star pair vs lone mid, 2-1), A6 (T11/T12, all-upper 3-1) and A8 (T15/T16, mid pair vs lone star) cells \u2014 48 of the 96 trials, so the binomial component of per-subject noise is small.

Predictions: under CG-VI-2 all discriminating weights clip to zero in A1 and A6, giving EXACTLY 0.500 there for every parameter setting (zero between-subject parameter variance), plus ~0.68 in A3 and ~0.87 in A8, so the pooled adherence lands near 0.63-0.65. Under GVIT the same experts carry negative weight, so the count winner is actively rejected in A1 (~0.25), A3 (~0.21) and A6 (~0.19) and only weakly followed in A8 (~0.59), giving pooled adherence near 0.30-0.33. Predicted gap ~0.30 in a quantity bounded in [0,1], with tight per-subject distributions (two of the four cells are parameter-free under CG, and the deliberately excluded floor-voice cells \u2014 A2, A4, A5, A7 \u2014 are the ones that carry most of each model's parameter-driven spread). Crucially it is not trivially true for CG: it would come out near chance or below if humans actually treat high-validity ratings as counter-indicative.

The two theories differ most sharply on displays whose tally-majority is carried by the panel's two star experts (f0=.92, f2=.84). CG-VI-2 floors news value at zero, so those stars are merely MUTE: for the unopposed star pair (C1, 2v0) and the all-upper 3v1 (C7) every discriminating weight clips to zero and P(choose the count winner) is exactly 0.500 by construction, while for the 2v1 star-pair cells (C3, C4) its weak chorus gate leaves positive evidence, so the majority is still followed above chance (~.60-.69). GVIT-CAP-S4 lets the weights go NEGATIVE, so on exactly these cells the star-backed majority is actively rejected (~.17-.22). Pooling only these four cells (48 trials per subject, mirrored A/B so side bias cancels) yields a predicted adherence of ~0.20 under GVIT versus ~0.57 under CG-VI-2 — a large mean gap, while the per-subject binomial noise over 48 trials is small and two of the four cells are parameter-free under CG, keeping between-subject variance tight. The metric is a simple proportion, well defined on both pooled and single-subject slices, and is not trivially true of my theory: it is a plain measure of following the unweighted cue count, which most standard accounts predict well above chance.

The two models disagree most sharply on two structurally opposite kinds of display, and in OPPOSITE directions, so a difference score amplifies the contrast while cancelling generic per-subject response noise.

(a) SOLO cells (C1 solo .95 star, C2 solo .75 mid; 24 trials/subject). CG-VI-2's chorus argument is CH = max(m)+|\u0394m|-2, so a lone discriminating voice gives CH=0, lam_eff=0, every weight exactly 1, z = beta (9.5-12.5): near-ceiling adherence ~0.94 regardless of the lone expert's validity. MBM-PG7 mutes any voice outside its narrow band unconditionally, so a lone star contributes only the thin residual eta -> ~0.54, and a lone mid ~0.71; mean ~0.63.

(b) FLAT cells (C4 unopposed .79/.75 pair, C5 low trio vs lone .95; 24 trials/subject). Here CH>=2 and every discriminating voice clips to exactly zero news value at every corner of CG's parameter box, so CG returns EXACTLY 0.500 even on a weakly dominant display and on a +2 tally margin. MBM keeps an inverse-seniority residual for muted voices and therefore follows the tally at ~0.70 / ~0.66.

Hence the composite (SOLO adherence - FLAT adherence) is predicted to be ~ +0.44 under CG-VI-2 but ~ -0.05 under MBM-PG7 (a near-zero/slightly negative value, since MBM actually follows the tally somewhat MORE in the dense cells than in the solo-star cell). Both terms are tight per subject: CG's solo term sits at ceiling (binomial var ~0.002 over 24 trials, parameter box only [0.91,0.96]) and its flat term is a parameter-free 0.5; MBM's terms are mid-range but its parameter box is narrow in both cells. The predicted between-theory gap (~0.5) is an order of magnitude larger than the expected per-subject SD (~0.11-0.14), giving a large Welch t at N=25. It is not trivially true of CG: any model that simply weights by validity, or that follows the plain tally, or that has graded (non-clipped) weights would produce a small or negative value here, since tally-following models score HIGH on the 2-vs-0 and 3-vs-1 cells.

The two models make structurally opposite predictions about WHEN the count winner is followed. CG-VI-2 releases all discounting for a solitary discriminating cue (chorus argument CH=0, so every weight = 1, z = beta), forcing near-ceiling adherence (~.94) on the solo-star and solo-low-upper cells; but for CH>=2 displays in which no panel-floor voice discriminates, its news values clip to exactly zero, giving E=0 and EXACTLY chance (.50) on the unopposed low pair (C4), the unopposed senior pair (C5) and the all-upper 3-vs-1 (C6), regardless of parameters. MBM-PG7 has no solo release (a lone star is still mute, contributing only the thin residual, ~.54; a lone low-upper ~.68) but its residual gradient keeps all-upper multi-cue displays clearly above chance (~.56-.67). The contrast [mean follow-rate on solo cells C1,C2] minus [mean follow-rate on all-upper cells C4,C5,C6] is therefore ~+0.44 under CG-VI-2 and ~-0.01 under MBM-PG7 -- a ~0.45 gap. Each cell contributes 12 trials per subject, the cells involved sit in the tightest parameter regions of both models (CG's C4/C5/C6 are parameter-free exact .50), so per-subject variance is dominated by binomial noise (~0.010-0.016), giving a Welch t of roughly 14 at N=25. Both theories' predictions here follow directly from their stated commitments rather than being trivially true of either.
